I know what I am going to say. First, I want to congratulate the minister on his appointment as minister in charge of the Crown corporation, and to thank him for his consideration in allowing me to take part in this debate. Under the new rules this can be done, but previously it would not have been as easy for me to rise as the first speaker from this side.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
The remarks I have to make are in no way intended as criticism of the minister. Of course, he has no department, he has no staff; he merely answers for a Crown corporation, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation. My remarks are directed to that corporation. I shall try to prove to him that all the good intentions expressed in his speech, as well as the intentions of the bill before us, will come to nothing if his tools are insufficient. I shall submit, and try to prove, that with the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation he will have a hard time getting anywhere.
Before I proceed, there is this question of whether the housing situation represents a crisis or a problem. I should like to give the house the benefit of my experience in this field. I have been actively engaged in housing construction for over 20 years. Whether this is a problem, a serious problem or a crisis does not mean very much. Calling it one or the other will not solve it. But I should like to identify it. Not only is there a shortage of houses in the metropolitan areas, but that shortage is aggravated by the fact that over the past 50 years the construction industry has built houses to last 30 years. There is therefore a continuing series of homes which can no longer be used.
There is a further difficulty. Seventy-five per cent of our people live in cities. In Toronto, to get decent accommodation-not fancy accommodation, just decent accommodation- the cost is 50 per cent of the take-home pay. Most Canadians will tolerate 25 per cent, but whether they pay rent or whether they own
National Housing Act
their own homes, 50 per cent is too much. For example, in Toronto one can rent what are called town houses-row houses with two or three bedrooms, a living room and so on, quite nice. Do hon. members know that a family has to earn between $9,000 and $10,000 a year to bring in $600 a month and that 50 per cent of this would go for rent? Actually, in this case the rent amounts to $283 a month, plus heating. This is really a crisis, because it affects a particular spectrum of people who have to rent or pay for accommodation. The man directly concerned has probably been working for a long time; he believes he is entitled to some good food, good clothing and so on. But now he finds he is living less well than he did ten years ago. And he is boiling. This is a serious problem.
It is senseless merely to say we have the best accommodation in the whole world. It is like saying the average depth of the Ottawa River is three feet, with the inference that one can walk across it. It is senseless. These are particular problems. They affect the people in the cities and they will eventually affect those in Montreal and other areas who at the present time are not suffering so much.
I wish to draw attention to one other aspect. There are many who do not understand the cause of these difficulties. A friend of mine remarked to me recently: I cannot understand this problem because I can buy a prefab house and put it on my land in the country somewhere at a cost of some $5,000. It would be a modest house, with two little bedrooms, a bathroom, a living room and so on, but it would serve. Of course, if people want automatic dishwashers, dryers and so on, they will have to pay for them; that is why their houses cost $35,000. If you tell people that they are entitled to yachts, they will want yachts; it is like saying to them "If there is no bread, eat cake".
But this man did not get to the root of the problem. The root of the problem is the cost of land. It is true one can buy a prefabricated house for $5,000 or $6,000, because the construction industry has kept up to date very well with regard to cost. But it is not true you can put such a house anywhere near a metropolitan area. When the price of land is running between $10,000 and $12,000 on the outskirts of a city and between $23,000 and $30,000 in Toronto itself, you cannot put a $6,000 house on it. The construction industry has kept up to date. In 1955 we were building homes for roughly $8.70 a square foot. Now, the cost is between $12 and $13. But when one considers the inflation which has taken

May 28, 1969
National Housing Act
place in the past 14 years and the type of house we are providing now, the cost is well in line. I think the construction industry has been extremely able. It has introduced mass production of stairways, kitchen units, windows, doors. It has even eliminated the hammering of nails by carpenters-that is all done automatically. The industry has tried to push ahead despite municipal restrictions, provincial restrictions and, in some cases, labour restrictions, and it has done a marvelous job in keeping costs down.
Nevertheless, it cannot provide a house at a low price when the cost of land is double the cost of construction. This is where the C.M.H.C. has failed. In the past month or so I have heard many comments on the housing situation. The word "housing" arouses a reflex action, it seems, in a lot of people in Canada. The word we hear is the word "constitution". I cannot understand for the life of me how we got into the constitutional question with regard to housing.

maintopic: TAXABLE INCOME ACCORDING TO MARITAL STATUS. DEPENDENTS AND INCOME FOR 1966
speechtext: Hear, hear.

maintopic: TAXABLE INCOME ACCORDING TO MARITAL STATUS. DEPENDENTS AND INCOME FOR 1966
speechtext:
One might think we were the only people who were keen to press on with housing. Mr. Speaker, I believe provincial and municipal politicians are as concerned as we are about this subject, if not more so. If on any issue we could hope to gain co-operation from the municipalities and the provinces without getting into a constitutional hassle, this would be the issue.
I looked at the National Housing Act, part five, for instance; having to do with housing research and community planning. I found that the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is allowed to do absolutely everything-everything they have done, and everything they may want to do. According to section 33 the corporation may, out of moneys advanced to it, bring about land or housing production by way of purchase, loans or otherwise, install or service any improvements to or in respect of any land required by it, and develop such land for housing purposes. Moreover, the corporation has power to manufacture windows, doors under this act. It has power to process lumber. Every conceivable power is there already, and how in the world we ever got into a constitutional hassle over this is a mystery to me. Had the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation been on its toes, had it been of any use whatsoever, we would never have been in this position.

Let us examine the position of C.M.H.C. as mortgage guarantors. The hon. member for Broadview (Mr. Gilbert) read a report by the president of the corporation in which he and his directors deplored the lack of money available. The hon. member for Broadview said the minister should act like King Canute holding back the tide. He thought he should legislate restrictively. But, Mr. Speaker, money knows no boundaries. It flows from nation to nation, taking the easiest course. Why does this happen?
In an article which appeared in the Globe and Mail on December 3 the president of the Life Insurance Association is reported as saying:
Canada needs a new type of financial institution similar to British building societies or U.S. mortgage loan associations to channel funds into mortgages.
He also said the insurance companies would be putting less and less money into mortgages, and that we could expect this to be the case. He expressed the view that it would be senseless for a mortgage company, a loan company or an insurance company to lend money at 7 per cent or even 9 per cent when the loss brought about by inflation alone was between 4 per cent and 5 per cent. Now, Mr. Speaker, until we try to control the inflationary cycle, this situation will be extremely hard to deal with. We have to keep the rise in wages and prices in line with the increase in the gross national product and until we do so, we shall not get very far. We shall not succeed in forcing anyone to do what we think they should do. The money will not be there.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
If the government were to say that it is not possible to have a wage and price increase of 9 per cent if the gross national product increases only 3 per cent-because this would mean 6 per cent inflation no matter which way you slice it-then we might get some co-operation wtih regard to investment. But you cannot force investment on the part of life insurance companies, or anybody else for that matter. They are buying equities because they are a hedge against inflation. They are competing with other life insurance companies in the United States who are selling insurance which offers real values. When they sell you a policy for $25,000 or $30,000 which matures in 35 or 50 years, you will receive a real value, not the current inflated dollar value. These companies have to meet and keep up with tough competition; as a result funds for mortgage purposes dry up.
May 28. 1969

Other sources of mortgage funds have been suggested. For example the building and loan societies that are common in Europe could be applicable here. It would need a littlte initiative on the part of Central Mortgage and Housing instead of their just decrying the lack of money. Loan and building societies encourage people to invest money and then buy a home. It is a co-operative arrangement and could apply to the trust and loan companies in Canada.
. Mr. McCleave: Could I put a question to the hon. member on this point about building societies. Is he not aware that the only one that existed in Canada, the Nova Scotia Savings and Loan Company, as it is presently known, altered its charter because it was found that the building society operation did not work in Canada?

maintopic: TAXABLE INCOME ACCORDING TO MARITAL STATUS. DEPENDENTS AND INCOME FOR 1966
speechtext: I have heard it said that nothing will work. The first answer you are given when you put forward an idea is that it just will not work. I say that other systems must be found.

speakerposition: N.D.P. House Leader; Whip of the N.D.P.
maintopic: TAXABLE INCOME ACCORDING TO MARITAL STATUS. DEPENDENTS AND INCOME FOR 1966
speechtext: That is what Adam said to Eve.

maintopic: TAXABLE INCOME ACCORDING TO MARITAL STATUS. DEPENDENTS AND INCOME FOR 1966
speechtext: They must be found and they can be found. As long as we keep believing that we are going to get $4 billion or $5 billion a year from life insurace companies we will not look at alternative sources.

maintopic: TAXABLE INCOME ACCORDING TO MARITAL STATUS. DEPENDENTS AND INCOME FOR 1966
speechtext: How much?

maintopic: TAXABLE INCOME ACCORDING TO MARITAL STATUS. DEPENDENTS AND INCOME FOR 1966
speechtext:
I said $4 billion or $5 billion a year. We will not investigate other methods if we believe we can get the money from this source.
Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has also been decrying the fact that private investors are not investing their money in areas outside large cities, that these rural areas have trouble getting insured loans. Has anyone ever asked why companies prefer to invest in the large metropolitan centres? The minister indicated to me privately that he knows why, but I am sure that C.M.H.C. does not know why-because they have never asked.
As the minister has pointed out, life insurance companies and other companies have no way of administering loans in small towns; as a result they do not want to expand their operations there. However, C.M.H.C. is empowered to administer mortgages and collect money. This they can do at a small charge. Consequently, there would be no
National Housing Act
problem in making money available in smaller areas.
As for land assemblers, the less said the better. Let me consider for a moment the role of research, for which we are going to give the corporation more money. I should like the minister to ask C.M.H.C. exactly what results have been produced during the last ten years. What new methods of construction have been approved? What new ideas have they accepted? I think the last one they accepted, and this with hesitancy, was the use of aluminum siding. But what have they done with this research money? We spend $39 million a year to keep C.M.H.C. operating.
For example, a little while ago I approached them with an idea in connection with sewage disposal. Sewage disposal systems, municipally organized and provincially administered, are at the crux of land cost. In Ontario there is the concept that all the sewage up from as far as Kapuskasing must come down through trunk sewers into Ashbridges Bay; otherwise the system will not work. Central Mortgage and Housing swallowed this concept hook, line and sinker. I read an article on a method of sewage disposal used in seven states which is more efficient-in fact, it is a miniature disposal plant-and can be installed by builders. It is bonded and guaranteed for 99 years. It cuts the cost from the present $1,300 a housing unit to $170 per unit if builders are allowed to develop the system. The effluent from this system is not even exuded into streams but is used in lawn sprinklers, and so on. It is made by a firm in Port Credit, near Toronto, but not one has been approved by C.M.H.C. because it would take them 20 years research to find out whether it would work.
If the periphery around Toronto were not tied to the trunk sewer system land would be available from one side of the city to the other. In that case the speculators would have nothing to speculate with. If one person wanted too much for his land, somebody else would sell it cheaper. With this system a builder would put in his own services. Many developers and builders would be glad to do this. They would like to put in schools, roads, the whole kit and caboodle, instead of having to pay high prices to speculators. But Central Mortgage and Housing do not think of this. They say that it is, after all, a municipal problem. The municipalities would dearly love some leadership in this regard because they cannot afford the cost of research.

May 28, 1969
National Housing Act
In the field of construction it is private industry that has made the changes and introduced the new ideas. Private industry has encountered much difficulty in getting these new concepts approved by Central Mortgage and Housing.
With regard to low rental housing, again I know the minister means well and wants more limited dividend housing loans. In this regard you must again work through C.M.H.C.
